extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, sociology, and political economy; thoughtful practitioners of politics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for investigating social and political phenomena: contrasting mistaken methods (chemical/experimental, geometrical/abstract) with the recommended concrete/deductive method and its verification, and guidance on scope, limits, and the separation of sociological subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the Chemical (Experimental) Method for complex social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chemical Method (experimental/elementary-chemistry-style) is a gross misconception when applied to political/social phenomena because it attempts to attribute effects to single causes by isolating variables in the manner of simple experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume you can subtract off all concurrent causes in social cases; experimental-style isolation is impracticable for most social phenomena because many causes act together. Experimental verification can only confirm conclusions drawn from general laws; rely on appropriate a priori reasoning about the effect of single causes only insofar as you account for the impossibility of isolating all other concurrent influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of the Geometrical (Abstract) Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Geometrical Method wrongly treats social science like geometry—deducing consequences from a few universal premises and assuming results from one principle cannot be altered by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructing social theories that treat each social phenomenon as resulting from a single cause or principle (e.g., rules based on 'abstract right' or a single practical maxim). Be wary of systems that ignore conflicts of forces, or assume truths proved from one principle remain unaffected by other principles; social phenomena involve many interacting causes and cannot be treated as co-existent, immutable geometrical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid founding political theory on unbending practical maxims or fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deducing political conclusions from unbending practical maxims (such as 'abstract right') or from fictions (like an assumed original social contract) is a fundamental misconception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use rules of conduct or assumed original obligations as premises for theory. Such approaches attempt to make an art into a deductive science and commit petitio principii by using practical precepts as theoretical foundations. Treat maxims as objects for theory to explain, not as axiomatic starting points for deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against single-principle political philosophies (e.g., interest-philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that explain social phenomena solely by one comprehensive premise (e.g., that all actions are determined by self-interest) are over-simplifications and often false when applied universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a single premise, limit its scope (e.g., to the conduct of large bodies or majorities) and acknowledge many other influences: habitual sentiments, traditions, class-based modes of thinking, predecessors' maxims. Do not infer far-reaching practical conclusions from such truncated foundations without allowances; lack of breadth in foundations misallocates attention and produces misleading superstructures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the Physical/Concrete Deductive Method for social science
rubrics_metrics.description: Social science should be deductive in the manner of the complex physical sciences (astronomy, natural philosophy): infer laws of effects from the laws of the separate elements and compound multiple causal laws to determine aggregate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning a priori, consider all causes that conjunctly influence an effect and compound their laws. Recognize that complexity makes a priori deduction more precarious here than in simpler sciences; therefore employ appropriate adaptations and precautions (see Verification). Use the concrete deductive method to determine tendencies and conditional theorems for particular sets of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification is an essential constituent of concrete deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification—collating deductive conclusions with concrete phenomena or their empirical laws—is the third essential part of the deductive method and the ground of confidence in concrete deductive sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a priori deduction alone. Use empirical observation to confirm, revise, or invert the order of reasoning when necessary (in some cases first obtain provisional laws from experience and then connect them with principles of human nature). The concurrence of deduction and observation justifies sociological conclusions despite complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits: sociology yields tendencies, not precise predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the multitude and variability of concurrent causes, sociology (as a system of a priori deductions) cannot make positive, precise predictions, but can indicate tendencies—how causes will operate unless counteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of tendencies for practical guidance and risk mitigation rather than expecting infallible forecasts. Frame conditional theorems tailored to the particular circumstances of a given society rather than universal laws. To approach concrete truth, incorporate a greater number of individualizing circumstances into reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: All general sociological propositions are hypothetical and conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions in social science are grounded on supposed sets of circumstances and declare how a given cause would operate under those suppositions; they are inherently hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting general theorems, state the assumed set of circumstances explicitly; test whether omitted circumstances might modify the asserted effect. Avoid asserting universal, context-free theorems; instead provide means to construct appropriate theorems for specific cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intermixture/consensus of laws across social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Social phenomena are characterized by an intermixture of laws—every social element influences and is influenced by others (a 'consensus'), so no social phenomenon can be fully isolated without considering the condition of the whole society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any social feature, consider its connections with other societal elements and the society's general state of civilization and history. Recognize that effects propagate and react across parts of the social body; neglecting such interactions leads to erroneous or incomplete accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate separation into branches (e.g., Political Economy) when immediate causes are mainly of one class
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible and necessary to study certain branches separately (such as political economy) when a class of social phenomena is mainly determined in the first resort by one kind of causes (e.g., desire of wealth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate branches for tractability only when the immediately determining causes are principally of one kind; still allow for later adjustments to account for modifying circumstances. Construct departmental sciences by ascertaining the effect due to the principal class of causes, then allow for interference from other classes of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the inverse (historical-generalization) method where direct deduction is inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: For some sociological inquiries of prodigious complication, direct a priori deduction is inapplicable; in those cases obtain best empirical laws by generalization from history and then connect them to human nature (Comte's inverse order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ historical generalization as a legitimate route to sociological laws when direct deduction cannot yield empirical laws; nevertheless, do not accept an unlimited inversion—there is scope for both direct and inverse methods, and choice depends on the nature of the inquiry.
